title: The Lost Rain Bell
markdown:
In the Sky Meadows the ground was not earth at all, but cloud so soft you could sink into it like the snuggliest pillow. Tansy the tiger cub lived there, stripes bright as if sunbeams had painted them on, and her purr was a happy little rumble, a tiny thunderstorm of delight. With her played Mallow the cloud sheep, wool spun from the whitest fluff, so soft it felt like breathing in a sweet dream. His bleats were the gentlest whisper of wind through cotton.

“Mallow,” Tansy purred, tail giving a merry flick as she bounced on sunny paws. “Can you feel that happy buzz? It tickles my whiskers. It must be almost time for the Great Weather Herd parade.”

Mallow blinked his large gentle eyes and let out an airy bleat. “The wind has been whispering of it for days. The clouds are arranging themselves into their most splendid parade-ready shapes, like fluffy dancers getting ready for the stage.”

The Weather Herd parade happened once a year, when the Sky Shepherds guided their rain clouds down to the world below. At the front, carried by the lead cloud-sheep, was the Rain Bell. Its chime told all the herds it was time to begin, and the whole sky hummed with anticipation.

“I can hardly wait,” Tansy said, doing a little leap that sent puff-balls of cloud drifting around her. “I want to see the Nimbus Nannies with their great rumbling thunder-sheep, and the Cirrus Sprites with their flocks of thin wispy clouds that look like painted feathers.”

“And the sound of the Rain Bell,” Mallow added softly, gaze drifting upward. “It is a song of promise.”

They trotted together, paws making soft thumps on the cloud-ground, toward the Great Cloud Perch — an extra-firm cloud shaped like a proud pedestal, where the Rain Bell usually rested, gleaming like a single perfect dewdrop catching the morning sun. Their happy bounces stilled. Tansy’s whiskers drooped. Mallow let out a small worried sigh. The perch was bare. Utterly, completely bare.

“Where is it?” Tansy whispered. Her bright stripes seemed to dim. A tremor rippled through her fur, from twitching nose to the tip of her tail, like a sudden cold draft on a warm day.

Mallow looked around, cloud-like eyes wide. “If the Rain Bell is lost, how will the Weather Herd know when to begin? The world below might miss its rain.” The thought made him feel as heavy and grey as a thundercloud.

“We have to find it,” Tansy declared, tiger spirit roaring up like a tiny happy volcano. “We’ll search every cloud. Every single fluffy one.”

Mallow, a little sheepish about such a huge adventure, nodded all the same. He knew his own gentle nature might be just what they needed. “I will help. My fluff is very good at catching the faintest whisper of a breeze, and I can see the smallest things that others might miss.”

They bounced and drifted from cloud to cloud, some like giant marshmallows, others like fields of whipped cream. Tansy’s stripes blurred as she bounded. Mallow floated, keen eyes scanning. The wisps of mist only giggled and swirled away. The sunbeams shimmered and offered no clues.

Their search led them to a peculiar beautiful part of the meadows. Here the clouds were not merely fluffy. They were spun like delicate threads of silver and moonlight, shimmering with a soft glow. The air itself hummed with a quiet sweet melody. High above them, nestled on a cloud shaped like a perfect smiling crescent moon, something glittered.

“Look,” Tansy pointed with an eager paw. “Is that it? It looks like it.”

It was the Rain Bell. Its silvery surface shimmered and twinkled, but it was tangled, caught fast in the gossamer threads of a hammock. Nestled inside that delicate hammock was a creature so soft, so delicate, it seemed woven from moonlight itself: a Moon Moth. Her wings were like stained-glass windows, catching and refracting the faint magical light.

As Tansy and Mallow drifted closer, the Moon Moth fluttered shyly. “Please don’t be cross with me,” she whispered, voice as soft as falling dew. “I borrowed it.”

Tansy tilted her head. The first sharp worry about the bell melted into curiosity. “You borrowed it? Why?”

The Moon Moth’s large liquid eyes sparkled with a touch of sadness. “The stars were restless last night. My lullaby felt too quiet to reach them. I thought the Rain Bell’s chime might help the sleepy stars drift off. I truly didn’t realize it was so important for the Weather Herd.” She wrung her pale antennae, looking utterly sorry.

Mallow drifted closer, full of understanding. He knew how important quiet songs could be. “It is a very important bell, little Moon Moth. Its sound tells the whole sky, from the highest cloud to the deepest valley, that the rain is coming to help everything grow.”

The Moon Moth looked down at the bell, now understanding its purpose. “I am so very sorry. I never meant to cause any trouble. I will help you untangle it right away. Please let me help.”

With the most careful delicate movements she began to loosen the shimmering threads that held the bell captive. Tansy stood by, ready to catch it should it slip, powerful paws poised. Mallow watched, offering soft encouraging bleats that sounded like little puffs of encouragement. The sound of the bell, even muffled by the threads, was still beautiful, like distant chimes heard on a very quiet evening.

With a last gentle tug the bell was free. The Moon Moth nudged it toward Tansy. “Here. Please take it. And thank you for understanding.”

Tansy took the Rain Bell, metal cool and smooth against her paws. She gave it a tentative shake. Ding-a-ling. The sound, clear and pure, echoed through the silent silver-spun clouds. It was a call the whole sky knew, from the highest wisps to the deepest shadows.

From far away they heard a low happy rumble. Then another. And another. The great clouds began to stir and gather, arranging themselves into magnificent grey shapes, ready for their important work. The Weather Herd was responding.

The Moon Moth smiled, a soft luminous glow spreading across her wings. “Thank you. And perhaps, one day, when the stars are restless again, I will ask the wind to carry my song to you, and you can share its beauty with the world in your own way.”

Tansy and Mallow waved goodbye, then raced back toward the Great Cloud Perch with the bell held high. By the time they set it on the pedestal the first Sky Shepherds had appeared. Tansy placed the bell into the lead cloud-sheep’s fleece, and Mallow gave it one last careful nudge so it sat true.

The parade began. Nimbus Nannies rolled past with their thunder-sheep. Cirrus Sprites drifted after, painting pale ribbons across the blue. Tansy and Mallow sat together on a pillowy cloud and watched. The Sky Meadows, which had once seemed only like fluffy fields, now felt like a place where even the smallest whisper of a song had its own part to play.

Far below, the first showers found the waiting seeds. Far above, the Moon Moth’s hammock swayed, empty of bells and full of her own quiet song. The echo of the chime lingered, bright as a dewdrop, kind as rain.
characters: Tansy (a tiger cub), Mallow (a cloud sheep)
